Subject: Dedicated capacity estimate for 64k context / model sizing

Hi Logan,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday. We want to move toward a committed dedicated pool for the next 12 months — primary use is our in-house LLM (70B-ish architecture) with heavy long-context workloads. High-level requirements:
- Sustained production qps: 6 requests/sec (steady state), with occasional peaks to 20 rps for short bursts
- Target p95 generation latency <= 400ms for short responses (~150 tokens)
- Typical prompt+response context: 64k tokens (we expect long retrieval + multi-turn history)
- Expected concurrency: 6 concurrent live sessions (avg), but peak concurrency planning for 20

Two asks: (1) a sizing estimate (how many reserved GPUs / pool configuration) for a dedicated deployment including KV cache sizing, and (2) options where we trade precision for capacity (quantization profiles, fallback models) and the expected savings.

I've attached a CSV with sample request size histogram and model profile (neurolytics_model_profile.csv). Can you get a ballpark by EOD Monday? Also include any risks for model-quality regressions if we push aggressive quantization.

Appreciate it — Sara
Sr. Director, Platform
NeuroLytics

Hi Sara — thanks for the data. Quick read-through and preliminary thoughts below; Karthik and Marissa, please fill in the detailed math and any conservative knobs we should apply.

Summary (short):
- Three recommended configurations (conservative / balanced / aggressive) with trade-offs:
  1) Conservative (FP16 resident weights, minimal quantization): higher model RAM and KV retained on GPU — best quality, higher reserved GPU count.
  2) Balanced (8-bit weight quantization, 3-way sharding, KV on-GPU with selective offload): reasonable quality vs cost; recommended as our standard committed offer.
  3) Aggressive (4-bit + KV offload + batching optimizations): lowest GPU count but higher risk and more ops to validate quality.

Key constraints driving GPU count: resident model sharding strategy, KV cache memory per concurrent session (which scales linearly with context length), and acceptable batch size for throughput. For 64k context the KV cache dominates.

Action items:
- Karthik: detailed per-option GPU math + assumptions, include p95 latency row and headroom for peaks.
- Marissa: handoff doc for ops (autoscale burst plan, monitoring/playbooks).
- Aditya: include incremental pricing delta for reserved + burst.

I'll send a follow-up with numbers. If you prefer a single recommended option today, we'd steer to the Balanced 8-bit plan as the default for committed customers.

— Logan

Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity estimate for 64k context / model sizing — detailed sizing and assumptions

Hi all — diving into the numbers. I pulled the CSV Sara attached and validated the median and peak request sizes. Below are the assumptions and the per-option GPU counts.

Assumptions (conservative rounding):
- Model family: 70B-class dense transformer (weight matrix footprint quoted from vendor/profile).
- Baselines: FP16 resident weights (unsharded) ~70 GB total; 8-bit quant (GEMMINT8-like) reduces resident weight footprint to ~24–28 GB depending on optimizer state removal; 4-bit approaches (QLoRA-style or AI quant libs) can reduce further to ~14–18 GB but require kernel/ops validation.
- Sharding: we plan sharded model across 3 GPUs for latency parity and KV locality (3-way model parallelism). Model_shard = quantized_model_size / 3.
- KV cache sizing (rough rule-of-thumb we validated on similar models): KV per active session ~= 0.8 GB per 1k tokens (includes keys+values and small activation overhead). This includes per-token storage scaled by hidden dim + 2 bytes per value for int16-style cache when offloaded, but reflects our memory layout and compression in prod runtime.
- Activation and workspace overhead per GPU: ~6–8 GB (varies by sequence length and batch).
- Target concurrency planning: steady-state concurrency 6; planning headroom to 20 concurrent sessions for peak periods. We size for steady + 30% headroom and provide burst capacity options.

Calculations (rounded):
Case A — Conservative (FP16, no quant)
- Resident model shard per GPU = 70 GB / 3 ~= 24 GB
- KV per session (64k) = 0.8 GB * 64 = 51.2 GB per session
- For 6 concurrent sessions KV_total = 51.2 * 6 = 307 GB (must be resident or offloaded across the pool)
- If we keep KV on-GPU for lowest latency, we'd need many GPUs purely to hold KV: with 80 GB-GPU (A100-80GB) the KV slices + model shard + workspace -> effective usable per GPU for KV ~= 45 GB after weights/workspace. That implies roughly 307 / 45 ~= 6.8 -> 7 GPUs just for KV plus model shards duplicated in placement -> realistic conservative pool = 18–22 A100-80GB GPUs to meet latency and shard placement with headroom.

Case B — Balanced (8-bit quant, 3-way sharding, selective KV offload) [RECOMMENDED]
- Resident model shard per GPU = 26 GB / 3 ~= 9 GB (we take 26 GB as median quantized footprint)
- KV per session (64k) = 51.2 GB (same as above)
- Strategy: keep hot KV for active sessions on-GPU but offload cold KV ranges to NVMe/host to reduce pressure (our runtime supports async eviction of older prefix tokens). Effective on-GPU KV per session tuned to 12–16 GB (hot window), remainder offloaded. So plan on-GPU KV per concurrent session ~= 14 GB.
- For 6 concurrent sessions on-GPU KV_total ~= 84 GB. Add model_shard + workspace per GPU. With A100-80GB we can pack model shard + workspace + 20–28 GB KV per GPU comfortably. Practical pool size: 8–10 A100-80GB GPUs for reserved capacity to satisfy steady-state with 30% headroom. For peaks (20 concurrent), autoscale to add 6–8 GPUs on burst pool.
- Latency expectations: p95 ~ 250–450ms depending on batch shaping; we can hit target <= 400ms with optimized batching and hot-KV placement.

Case C — Aggressive (4-bit quant + KV offload + tight batching)
- Resident model shard per GPU ~= 16 GB / 3 ~= 5.3 GB
- Keep only very small hot KV on-GPU (4–6 GB/session), majority offloaded. This reduces reserved pool but increases p95 variance and increases SRE complexity.
- Practical reserved pool: 5–6 A100-80GB GPUs for steady-state; but plan for rapid autoscale and stricter quality gates.

Operational notes / risks:
- Quality risk: 8-bit quant typically introduces small decoding-quality deltas; we recommend an eval suite (sample prompts + human eval) to validate. 4-bit requires more careful per-layer validation and sometimes small fine-tuning or quant-aware calibration to avoid hallucinations on long-context recency.
- KV offload impact: offload introduces tail-latency variance; for strict p95 SLOs we keep a larger hot-KV window on-GPU and prioritize requests pinned to GPUs that hold their hot prefix.
- Burst strategy: commit to reserved pool (Balanced plan: 8–10 GPUs) + burst pool (on-demand) up to additional 8 GPUs. We can enforce billing caps and auto-failover to a smaller context model (e.g., 32k variant) when capacity is constrained.

Pricing & next steps (high-level):
- Estimated committed reserved A100-80GB GPUs: 8 GPUs (balanced) — ballpark pricing and committed discount options to be included in formal proposal. Aditya will attach pricing tiers in the proposal.
- Deliverables: detailed capacity worksheet (kv_cache_calc.xlsx), ops runbook draft, and a draft contract for reserved capacity + burst credits.

Attachments: kv_cache_calc.xlsx (per-session breakdown and GPU-fit matrix), draft proposal redwood_dedicated_proposal_v1.pdf

I'll hand the ops points to Marissa for a short runbook.

-Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Principal Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
